content.summary: Welcome to the reading sub-module for Unit A2.2-M03. In this lesson, you will read about important life milestones and personal experiences. You will learn how to use the present perfect tense with just, already, and yet to talk about recent actions and completed goals.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Present perfect tense with just, already, and yet in affirmative, negative, and interrogative sentences.

contextWarmup.prompt: When someone finishes university or gets their first job, what do we call this important event in English?
contextWarmup.explanation: Getting a degree or starting a career is an important milestone in a person's life.

rules: JUST is used for actions that happened very recently. Formula: Subject plus have or has plus just plus past participle. Example: I have just finished my exam.
ALREADY is used to show something happened sooner than expected. Formula: Subject plus have or has plus already plus past participle. Example: She has already graduated from university.

YET is used in questions to ask if something happened, or in negative sentences to show it has not happened. Formula: Have or has plus subject plus past participle plus yet, or subject plus haven't or hasn't plus past participle plus yet. Example: Have you found a job yet?

commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use yet in affirmative sentences to mean already. Remember that yet only belongs in questions and negative sentences.
commonTrap.wrong: I have finished my homework yet.
commonTrap.correct: I have already finished my homework, or I haven't finished my homework yet.

Her family is very proud because she has already found a full-time job at an international company. Anna says that getting the job was her biggest achievement so far.

However, Anna still has many goals to accomplish. She has just moved into a small apartment near her new office, but she has not unpacked all her boxes yet. She also wants to buy a car, but she has not decided which model to choose yet. Life moves fast, and Anna is excited about her future adventures.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Life Milestones with Present Perfect

content.summary: Practical guide on writing about life milestones and experiences using the present perfect tense with just, already, and yet in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Using 'Just' for Recent Actions
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have / has + just + past participle
blueprintItems.example: I have just finished my university degree.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Using 'Already' for Early Actions
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have / has + already + past participle
blueprintItems.example: She has already bought her first car.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Using 'Yet' in Questions and Negatives
blueprintItems.formula: Have / Has + subject + past participle + yet? OR Subject + haven't / hasn't + past participle + yet
blueprintItems.example: Have you found a job yet? I haven't started working yet.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of sentences and proper nouns such as names, cities, and countries.
mechanicsRules.badExample: i have just visited london with my friend anna.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I have just visited London with my friend Anna.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences begin with capital letters, and cities and names are proper nouns.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place 'just' and 'already' between auxiliary verbs and past participles.
mechanicsRules.badExample: They have finished already their project.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: They have already finished their project.
mechanicsRules.why: In English word order, adverbs like already and just sit before the main past participle verb.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always place 'yet' at the end of negative sentences and questions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: We yet haven't bought a new house.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We haven't bought a new house yet.
mechanicsRules.why: The adverb yet is positioned at the end of negative statements and interrogative sentences.

content.summary: Learn how to speak about life milestones and experiences using the Present Perfect tense with just, already, and yet. Focus on natural word stress, linking auxiliary verbs like have and has, and maintaining clear intonation when sharing personal updates.
content.audioGuidance: Pay attention to how auxiliary verbs are reduced in spoken English. For example, 'I have' sounds like 'I've', and 'has' is often unstressed before past participles.

pillars.name: Auxiliary Reduction
pillars.target: Smooth contraction of have and has
pillars.explanation: In natural speech, 'I have' becomes 'I've' and 'she has' becomes 'she's' to maintain smooth rhythm.

pillars.name: Adverb Placement Stress
pillars.explanation: Place mild stress on adverbs like just and already to emphasize timing in your achievements.
